note: Pathology Live photoreal specimens for the cc engine diseases. Add a complication by copying an entry: id is "<disease>-<complication>" and must match cc/db.json. organ is lung, kidney, heart, liver, brain, vessel, pancreas, muscle, skin, bowel or bleed. Set glb to a .glb/.gltf path to replace the gross specimen. picks["*"] and picks["**"] replace the tap-to-inspect text in gross and cell views. No viewer code change is needed for a new entry that reuses an organ.

complications.title: RV failure in ARDS

views.label: Heart
views.text: The right ventricle dilates against a high-resistance lung circulation and bows the septum toward the left.

views.label: Chamber
views.text: The right cavity is large and thin-walled. The septum is flattened, which squeezes the left ventricle.

views.label: Myocyte
views.text: Right ventricular muscle cells are over stretched and their coronary supply falls under pressure. Stretch and ischaemia signals cut the force each cell can generate.

*.body: High resistance in the lung circulation overloads the thin walled right ventricle. It dilates and pushes the septum toward the left ventricle, so left filling and cardiac output fall.
*.care: Helps: Lung protective ventilation; Prone positioning; Inhaled nitric oxide. Avoid: Excess PEEP and plateau pressure; Large fluid bolus.

**.body: Right ventricular muscle cells are over stretched and their coronary supply falls under pressure. Stretch and ischaemia signals cut the force each cell can generate.
**.care: Helps: Lung protective ventilation; Prone positioning; Inhaled nitric oxide. Avoid: Excess PEEP and plateau pressure; Large fluid bolus.

complications.reversibleText: Often reversible once oxygenation, pH and driving pressure improve. Prolonged ARDS can leave chronic pulmonary hypertension.

complications.title: Barotrauma in ARDS

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Over-distended lung with surface blebs. Air escapes from torn alveoli into the pleura or the mediastinum.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Stiff, patchy lung with air-filled blebs under the pleura and interstitial air along vessels.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: Over stretched alveolar cells and their walls rupture. Mechanical stress signals also trigger inflammation, a process called biotrauma.

*.body: Excess ventilator pressure or volume tears the lung. Air escapes into the pleura and mediastinum, and a pneumothorax can collapse the lung and stop the circulation.
*.care: Helps: Low tidal volume, 6 ml per kg; Plateau pressure under 30; Neuromuscular blockade. Avoid: High tidal volume; Excess PEEP.

**.body: Over stretched alveolar cells and their walls rupture. Mechanical stress signals also trigger inflammation, a process called biotrauma.
**.care: Helps: Low tidal volume, 6 ml per kg; Plateau pressure under 30; Neuromuscular blockade. Avoid: High tidal volume; Excess PEEP.

complications.reversibleText: Air leaks heal once pressure falls; a tension pneumothorax needs immediate decompression and is fatal if missed.

complications.title: Fibrosis after ARDS

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Pale, firm, shrunken lung with a coarse surface. Scar replaces functioning air space.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Grey-white fibrous bands and small honeycomb cysts in place of spongy lung.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: Fibroblasts proliferate and lay down collagen in the walls and air spaces. The thickened wall slows gas movement and the alveoli cannot stretch.

*.body: After the acute phase some lungs fail to heal. The lung becomes stiff and shrunken, gas transfer is poor, and the patient stays ventilator dependent.
*.care: Helps: Corticosteroids in selected late ARDS; Lung protective ventilation; Conservative fluid strategy. Avoid: Prolonged high oxygen; Late high pressure ventilation.

**.body: Fibroblasts proliferate and lay down collagen in the walls and air spaces. The thickened wall slows gas movement and the alveoli cannot stretch.
**.care: Helps: Corticosteroids in selected late ARDS; Lung protective ventilation; Conservative fluid strategy. Avoid: Prolonged high oxygen; Late high pressure ventilation.

complications.reversibleText: Early fibroproliferation can partly resolve. Established collagen scar usually persists, and many survivors have lasting lung function loss.

complications.title: Ventilator-associated pneumonia

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Dependent lobes are heavy, dull red and airless. Pus fills the bronchioles.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: The cut surface is granular and yellow-red. Purulent material can be squeezed from small airways.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: Bacteria colonise the alveoli and neutrophils and macrophages flood in. They release enzymes and cytokines that injure alveolar and capillary cells and fill the sacs with pus.

*.body: Bacteria enter the lower airway around the tube. A patch of lung consolidates, secretions turn purulent, and oxygenation worsens after a period of improvement.
*.care: Helps: Head of bed up 30 to 45 degrees; Subglottic suction and cuff pressure care; Daily sedation hold and weaning review. Avoid: Lying flat; Prolonged ventilation without weaning review.

**.body: Bacteria colonise the alveoli and neutrophils and macrophages flood in. They release enzymes and cytokines that injure alveolar and capillary cells and fill the sacs with pus.
**.care: Helps: Head of bed up 30 to 45 degrees; Subglottic suction and cuff pressure care; Daily sedation hold and weaning review. Avoid: Lying flat; Prolonged ventilation without weaning review.

complications.reversibleText: Treatable with early appropriate antibiotics. Delay raises mortality and prolongs ventilation.

complications.title: Shock in acute pancreatitis

views.label: Microvessels
views.text: Capillaries leak into the retroperitoneum. Tissue becomes wet and pale while vessels dilate.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Wet, oedematous tissue with wide capillaries. Fluid sits between the cells.

views.label: Capillary
views.text: Cytokines such as TNF and IL 6 loosen the junctions between endothelial cells. Plasma escapes, tissue cells swell, and low oxygen delivery pushes them toward anaerobic metabolism.

*.body: Fluid leaks from the capillaries into the retroperitoneum and the third space. Blood volume and pressure fall, and organs lose perfusion.
*.care: Helps: Early balanced crystalloid; Noradrenaline. Avoid: Excessive fluids; Starch fluids.

**.body: Cytokines such as TNF and IL 6 loosen the junctions between endothelial cells. Plasma escapes, tissue cells swell, and low oxygen delivery pushes them toward anaerobic metabolism.
**.care: Helps: Early balanced crystalloid; Noradrenaline. Avoid: Excessive fluids; Starch fluids.

complications.reversibleText: Usually reversible with early volume and vasopressor support. Shock from infected necrosis is harder to reverse.

complications.title: ARDS from pancreatitis

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Enzymes and cytokines from the gland injure the alveolar wall. Both bases flood first.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Dark red, heavy lung. Fluid and hyaline membranes fill the dependent air spaces.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: Cytokines and activated neutrophils injure the capillary and alveolar cells. Protein rich fluid enters the air spaces and surfactant is lost.

*.body: Inflammatory mediators from the pancreas reach the lungs through the blood. Both lungs flood and stiffen, and the oxygen level falls.
*.care: Helps: Lung protective ventilation; Prone positioning; Conservative fluids after resuscitation. Avoid: Excess fluid; High tidal volume.

**.body: Cytokines and activated neutrophils injure the capillary and alveolar cells. Protein rich fluid enters the air spaces and surfactant is lost.
**.care: Helps: Lung protective ventilation; Prone positioning; Conservative fluids after resuscitation. Avoid: Excess fluid; High tidal volume.

complications.reversibleText: Often reversible over days to weeks if the pancreatic inflammation settles.

complications.title: AKI in acute pancreatitis

views.label: Kidney
views.text: The kidney swells and the cortex pales. Low volume and a high abdominal pressure cut the perfusion.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pale cortex and congested medulla. Tubular necrosis shows as pale streaks.

views.label: Tubule
views.text: Tubule cells are short of oxygen and energy. They lose their brush border, detach into the lumen and block the flow.

*.body: Low volume and high abdominal pressure cut kidney perfusion. Urine output falls and creatinine rises, with potassium, acid and urea building up.
*.care: Helps: Early volume resuscitation; Avoid NSAIDs and contrast; Decompress abdominal hypertension. Avoid: NSAID analgesia; Aminoglycoside.

**.body: Tubule cells are short of oxygen and energy. They lose their brush border, detach into the lumen and block the flow.
**.care: Helps: Early volume resuscitation; Avoid NSAIDs and contrast; Decompress abdominal hypertension. Avoid: NSAID analgesia; Aminoglycoside.

complications.reversibleText: Usually reversible if perfusion is restored early. Prolonged injury can cause tubular necrosis or chronic kidney disease.

complications.title: Pancreatic necrosis

views.label: Pancreas
views.text: The gland is swollen, with chalky fat necrosis and dark haemorrhage. Peripancreatic fluid collects around it.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Cream-yellow dead lobules with dark red haemorrhage. Dead tissue does not enhance on a scan.

views.label: Acinus
views.text: Calcium overload and mitochondrial failure activate trypsin inside the acinar cell. The membrane ruptures and the enzymes digest neighbouring cells.

*.body: Part of the gland and the fat around it die. Dead tissue releases enzymes and cytokines, can become infected, and drives organ failure.
*.care: Helps: Oxygen and perfusion support; Early enteral nutrition; ERCP for gallstone with cholangitis. Avoid: Early surgical debridement; Aggressive fluids.

**.body: Calcium overload and mitochondrial failure activate trypsin inside the acinar cell. The membrane ruptures and the enzymes digest neighbouring cells.
**.care: Helps: Oxygen and perfusion support; Early enteral nutrition; ERCP for gallstone with cholangitis. Avoid: Early surgical debridement; Aggressive fluids.

complications.reversibleText: Dead tissue does not recover. The gland may heal around it, but necrosis can become infected and need drainage.

complications.title: Abdominal compartment syndrome

views.label: Bowel
views.text: Bowel loops are oedematous and distended. Pressure inside the abdomen squeezes the vessels of the gut wall.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Thick, wet bowel wall and dusky mucosa. Venous return and gut perfusion both fall.

views.label: Villus
views.text: High pressure squeezes the small vessels in the gut wall and kidney. Cells downstream lose blood flow, swell and switch to anaerobic metabolism, and the gut barrier fails.

*.body: Fluid and swollen bowel raise the pressure inside the abdomen above 20 mmHg. The diaphragm is pushed up, venous return falls and the kidneys and gut lose blood flow.
*.care: Helps: Sedation and neuromuscular blockade; Gastric decompression; Percutaneous drainage of ascites. Avoid: Further large fluid boluses; Tight abdominal binder.

**.body: High pressure squeezes the small vessels in the gut wall and kidney. Cells downstream lose blood flow, swell and switch to anaerobic metabolism, and the gut barrier fails.
**.care: Helps: Sedation and neuromuscular blockade; Gastric decompression; Percutaneous drainage of ascites. Avoid: Further large fluid boluses; Tight abdominal binder.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible with decompression. Delay causes kidney, gut and liver ischaemia.

complications.title: Hypocalcaemia in pancreatitis

views.label: Pancreas
views.text: Calcium soaps form in the dead fat around the gland. That binds calcium and the serum level falls.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: White, chalky specks in the fat. They are fatty acids bound to calcium.

views.label: Acinus
views.text: Low outside calcium makes sodium channels open too easily. Nerve and muscle cells fire spontaneously, causing tetany and arrhythmia.

*.body: Calcium soaps form in the dead fat around the pancreas and calcium falls in the blood. The patient has tingling, cramps and a long QT interval, and may have seizures.
*.care: Helps: IV calcium gluconate; Magnesium replacement; Treat the pancreatitis and correct for albumin. Avoid: Citrate rich blood products.

**.body: Low outside calcium makes sodium channels open too easily. Nerve and muscle cells fire spontaneously, causing tetany and arrhythmia.
**.care: Helps: IV calcium gluconate; Magnesium replacement; Treat the pancreatitis and correct for albumin. Avoid: Citrate rich blood products.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible with calcium and magnesium. It usually settles as the pancreatitis resolves.

complications.title: Hyperkalaemia in AKI

views.label: Heart
views.text: The heart looks normal to the eye. The danger is electrical: potassium depolarises the muscle and the rhythm fails.

views.label: Chamber
views.text: No gross change. The risk is a slow, wide rhythm that ends in asystole or ventricular fibrillation.

views.label: Myocyte
views.text: High outside potassium makes the resting membrane potential less negative. Sodium channels inactivate, so cells fire poorly and conduction slows.

*.body: The kidney cannot excrete potassium. The heart is at risk first: tall T waves, a wide QRS, then ventricular arrhythmia or arrest.
*.care: Helps: IV calcium gluconate; Insulin with glucose; Nebulised salbutamol. Avoid: Potassium supplements or ACE inhibitor.

**.body: High outside potassium makes the resting membrane potential less negative. Sodium channels inactivate, so cells fire poorly and conduction slows.
**.care: Helps: IV calcium gluconate; Insulin with glucose; Nebulised salbutamol. Avoid: Potassium supplements or ACE inhibitor.

complications.reversibleText: Rapidly reversible with treatment, but untreated severe hyperkalaemia causes fatal arrhythmia.

complications.title: Metabolic acidosis in AKI

views.label: Kidney
views.text: The kidney cannot excrete acid or make new bicarbonate. Injury is tubular and reduces ammonium output.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pale cortex and congested medulla. The failure is chemical, so the gross change is mild.

views.label: Tubule
views.text: Tubule cells normally secrete hydrogen ions and generate bicarbonate. Injured cells cannot, so acid accumulates and inhibits enzymes and the sodium potassium pump.

*.body: The kidney cannot excrete acid or make new bicarbonate. The pH falls, breathing becomes deep and fast, and the heart responds poorly to catecholamines.
*.care: Helps: Treat the cause, restore perfusion; Renal replacement therapy; Sodium bicarbonate for pH below 7.2. Avoid: Large volumes of saline; Metformin continued.

**.body: Tubule cells normally secrete hydrogen ions and generate bicarbonate. Injured cells cannot, so acid accumulates and inhibits enzymes and the sodium potassium pump.
**.care: Helps: Treat the cause, restore perfusion; Renal replacement therapy; Sodium bicarbonate for pH below 7.2. Avoid: Large volumes of saline; Metformin continued.

complications.reversibleText: Reverses as kidney function returns or with dialysis. Severe acidosis impairs the heart and the response to vasopressors.

complications.title: Pulmonary oedema in AKI

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Salt and water retained by the kidney flood the lungs. Both lungs are heavy and wet.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Frothy pink fluid runs from the cut surface. The lung is wet and heavy.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: High pressure forces fluid across the capillary wall. Type 2 alveolar cells that clear the fluid cannot keep up, so the sacs fill and gas exchange stops.

*.body: When the kidney cannot remove salt and water, volume overload raises pressure in the lung capillaries. Fluid enters the air spaces and the patient becomes breathless.
*.care: Helps: Ultrafiltration or dialysis; Loop diuretic, if still making urine; Non invasive ventilation. Avoid: Further IV fluids.

**.body: High pressure forces fluid across the capillary wall. Type 2 alveolar cells that clear the fluid cannot keep up, so the sacs fill and gas exchange stops.
**.care: Helps: Ultrafiltration or dialysis; Loop diuretic, if still making urine; Non invasive ventilation. Avoid: Further IV fluids.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible once volume is removed by diuresis or ultrafiltration.

complications.title: Uraemia in AKI

views.label: Kidney
views.text: Urea and other solutes build up as filtration falls. The kidney is swollen and pale.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pale swollen cortex. The harm comes from retained toxins in the blood, not from the kidney itself.

views.label: Tubule
views.text: Retained toxins disturb the membranes and enzymes of platelets, neurons and the pericardial lining. Platelets lose their stickiness and neurons signal poorly.

*.body: Urea and other waste solutes accumulate. The patient becomes nauseated and drowsy, bleeds easily and may develop pericarditis or seizures.
*.care: Helps: Dialysis; Treat acidosis and anaemia. Avoid: Delaying dialysis despite encephalopathy or pericarditis; Accumulating sedatives and opioids.

**.body: Retained toxins disturb the membranes and enzymes of platelets, neurons and the pericardial lining. Platelets lose their stickiness and neurons signal poorly.
**.care: Helps: Dialysis; Treat acidosis and anaemia. Avoid: Delaying dialysis despite encephalopathy or pericarditis; Accumulating sedatives and opioids.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible with dialysis, though the cause of AKI must also recover.

complications.title: Cerebral oedema in acute liver failure

views.label: Brain
views.text: Flattened gyri and narrowed sulci. Ammonia is converted to glutamine in astrocytes, which swell with water.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Grey and white matter lose their distinction. The brain is soft, wet and bulging.

views.label: Neurone and barrier
views.text: Astrocytes convert ammonia to glutamine. Glutamine is osmotic, so astrocytes swell, and mitochondrial injury makes it worse.

*.body: Ammonia rises because the liver cannot clear it. The brain swells inside the rigid skull, the pressure rises and the patient may herniate.
*.care: Helps: Hypertonic saline; Mannitol; Head up 30 degrees. Avoid: Hypotonic fluids; Fever and low sodium.

**.body: Astrocytes convert ammonia to glutamine. Glutamine is osmotic, so astrocytes swell, and mitochondrial injury makes it worse.
**.care: Helps: Hypertonic saline; Mannitol; Head up 30 degrees. Avoid: Hypotonic fluids; Fever and low sodium.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible if ammonia and pressure are controlled early; herniation is often fatal.

complications.title: Hypoglycaemia in acute liver failure

views.label: Liver
views.text: The liver cannot make glucose from glycogen or by gluconeogenesis. It is swollen and mottled with necrosis.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Mottled red and yellow surface with patchy or confluent necrosis. Glycogen stores are gone.

views.label: Hepatocytes
views.text: Hepatocytes lose their glycogen stores and cannot make new glucose from amino acids. Failing mitochondria cut the energy that gluconeogenesis needs.

*.body: The liver normally releases glucose between meals. In liver failure it cannot, so glucose falls and causes confusion, seizures and coma that can be mistaken for encephalopathy.
*.care: Helps: IV dextrose; N acetylcysteine in paracetamol or non paracetamol ALF. Avoid: Fasting without dextrose; Insulin or sulfonylurea.

**.body: Hepatocytes lose their glycogen stores and cannot make new glucose from amino acids. Failing mitochondria cut the energy that gluconeogenesis needs.
**.care: Helps: IV dextrose; N acetylcysteine in paracetamol or non paracetamol ALF. Avoid: Fasting without dextrose; Insulin or sulfonylurea.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible with glucose; recurrent hypoglycaemia in ALF is a sign of poor liver reserve and a bad prognosis.

complications.title: Coagulopathy in acute liver failure

views.label: Soft tissue
views.text: The liver makes most clotting factors. When it fails, bruises and bleeding appear from sites that would normally seal.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Haematoma in soft tissue and oozing from every puncture site.

views.label: Capillary wall
views.text: Hepatocytes stop making factors II, V, VII, IX and X and fibrinogen. Platelets fall and fibrinolysis is altered, so clots form poorly.

*.body: The liver makes most clotting factors. In failure the INR rises and the patient bleeds from the gums, gut and lines, even though platelets also fall.
*.care: Helps: Vitamin K; Plasma, only for bleeding or procedures; Platelets or cryoprecipitate for bleeding. Avoid: Routine plasma to correct INR; NSAIDs or antiplatelets.

**.body: Hepatocytes stop making factors II, V, VII, IX and X and fibrinogen. Platelets fall and fibrinolysis is altered, so clots form poorly.
**.care: Helps: Vitamin K; Plasma, only for bleeding or procedures; Platelets or cryoprecipitate for bleeding. Avoid: Routine plasma to correct INR; NSAIDs or antiplatelets.

complications.reversibleText: Recovers as the liver recovers. INR is a marker of liver function, so it is corrected only for bleeding or before procedures.

complications.title: Hepatorenal AKI

views.label: Kidney
views.text: The kidney looks structurally normal, but flow is low. Splanchnic vasodilation drops the effective arterial volume.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: The kidney is mildly pale. Histology is often near-normal because the problem is haemodynamic.

views.label: Tubule
views.text: Renin, angiotensin and noradrenaline constrict the supply to the glomerulus. Tubule cells are intact at first but run short of oxygen if low flow persists.

*.body: Vasodilation in the gut lowers the effective circulating volume. The kidney constricts to protect pressure, so filtration falls and the urine becomes almost sodium free, even though the kidney is structurally normal.
*.care: Helps: Terlipressin or noradrenaline with albumin; Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins; Treat infection. Avoid: NSAIDs; Large volume paracentesis without albumin.

**.body: Renin, angiotensin and noradrenaline constrict the supply to the glomerulus. Tubule cells are intact at first but run short of oxygen if low flow persists.
**.care: Helps: Terlipressin or noradrenaline with albumin; Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins; Treat infection. Avoid: NSAIDs; Large volume paracentesis without albumin.

complications.reversibleText: Often reversible if the liver recovers or with transplant. Renal replacement can bridge.

complications.title: Infection and vasoplegia in acute liver failure

views.label: Microvessels
views.text: Dilated, slow capillaries with leaky walls. Failing Kupffer cells make infection more likely.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Wet tissue with wide capillaries. Perfusion pressure is low despite a high cardiac output.

views.label: Capillary
views.text: Impaired liver clearance of bacteria and endotoxin lets cytokines surge. Nitric oxide relaxes vascular smooth muscle and the endothelium leaks.

*.body: Failing Kupffer cells and low complement leave the patient open to bacterial and fungal infection. Sepsis and vasodilation cause shock, and the infection can bring on brain swelling.
*.care: Helps: Early cultures and broad antibiotics; Noradrenaline; Antifungal cover when indicated. Avoid: Delayed antibiotics; Excess fluid in vasoplegia.

**.body: Impaired liver clearance of bacteria and endotoxin lets cytokines surge. Nitric oxide relaxes vascular smooth muscle and the endothelium leaks.
**.care: Helps: Early cultures and broad antibiotics; Noradrenaline; Antifungal cover when indicated. Avoid: Delayed antibiotics; Excess fluid in vasoplegia.

complications.reversibleText: Treatable if recognised early. Infection is a leading cause of death and can worsen brain swelling.

complications.title: Pulmonary oedema in heart failure

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Back-pressure from the left ventricle forces fluid into the air spaces. The lungs are heavy and wet.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pink froth runs from the cut surface. Alveoli are filled with fluid.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: High pressure in the lung capillaries forces fluid across the thin wall and breaks it. The alveoli fill and gas exchange falls.

*.body: The failing left ventricle cannot empty, so pressure backs up into the lungs. The patient is breathless and may cough pink frothy sputum.
*.care: Helps: Non invasive ventilation; IV loop diuretic; Nitrates. Avoid: Morphine; IV fluid bolus.

**.body: High pressure in the lung capillaries forces fluid across the thin wall and breaks it. The alveoli fill and gas exchange falls.
**.care: Helps: Non invasive ventilation; IV loop diuretic; Nitrates. Avoid: Morphine; IV fluid bolus.

complications.reversibleText: Often rapidly reversible with decongestion and afterload reduction.

complications.title: Cardiogenic shock

views.label: Heart
views.text: A dilated, pale ventricle that cannot eject. Ischaemic muscle is mottled and soft.

views.label: Chamber
views.text: The cavity is dilated and the wall is thin. Pale or dusky areas mark infarcted muscle.

views.label: Myocyte
views.text: Myocytes lack energy and calcium handling fails, so contraction weakens. Inflammatory signals and nitric oxide dilate vessels and deepen the shock.

*.body: The ventricle cannot pump enough blood. Pressure falls, the skin turns cold, and the kidneys, liver and brain lose perfusion.
*.care: Helps: Revascularisation; Noradrenaline; Dobutamine. Avoid: Beta blocker; Large fluid bolus.

**.body: Myocytes lack energy and calcium handling fails, so contraction weakens. Inflammatory signals and nitric oxide dilate vessels and deepen the shock.
**.care: Helps: Revascularisation; Noradrenaline; Dobutamine. Avoid: Beta blocker; Large fluid bolus.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible only if the cause, such as an occluded artery, is corrected quickly. Delay leads to multi organ failure.

complications.title: Cardiorenal AKI

views.label: Kidney
views.text: Low output and high venous pressure both reduce kidney perfusion. The organ is congested and pale.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Congested, dark medulla with pale cortex. Venous congestion swells the capsule.

views.label: Tubule
views.text: Tubule cells are short of oxygen under low flow and congestion. Neurohormonal activation adds vasoconstriction and sodium retention.

*.body: Low output cuts kidney blood flow, while venous congestion raises back pressure in the renal veins. Both lower filtration.
*.care: Helps: Restore cardiac output; Decongestion with diuretic; Avoid nephrotoxins. Avoid: ACE inhibitor in shock; NSAIDs.

**.body: Tubule cells are short of oxygen under low flow and congestion. Neurohormonal activation adds vasoconstriction and sodium retention.
**.care: Helps: Restore cardiac output; Decongestion with diuretic; Avoid nephrotoxins. Avoid: ACE inhibitor in shock; NSAIDs.

complications.reversibleText: Usually reversible if the heart recovers; persistent low output causes tubular necrosis.

complications.title: Arrhythmia in heart failure

views.label: Heart
views.text: A dilated, scarred ventricle is the substrate. A fast rhythm shortens filling and drops output further.

views.label: Chamber
views.text: Patchy scar within the wall acts as a circuit for re-entry.

views.label: Myocyte
views.text: Stretched and ischaemic cardiomyocytes depolarise early and unevenly. Calcium handling becomes disordered, so electrical waves re enter and circle the muscle.

*.body: A fast or irregular rhythm shortens filling time and the loss of atrial kick drops output. A failing heart may decompensate within hours.
*.care: Helps: Treat triggers: ischaemia, potassium, magnesium; Synchronised cardioversion if unstable; Amiodarone for rate control. Avoid: Calcium blocker or beta blocker bolus in decompensated failure; Excess inotrope.

**.body: Stretched and ischaemic cardiomyocytes depolarise early and unevenly. Calcium handling becomes disordered, so electrical waves re enter and circle the muscle.
**.care: Helps: Treat triggers: ischaemia, potassium, magnesium; Synchronised cardioversion if unstable; Amiodarone for rate control. Avoid: Calcium blocker or beta blocker bolus in decompensated failure; Excess inotrope.

complications.reversibleText: Often reversible with correction of the trigger. Unstable rhythms need immediate cardioversion.

complications.title: Raised intracranial pressure

views.label: Brain
views.text: The brain swells inside a rigid skull. Gyri flatten and sulci close.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: The ventricles are compressed and the grey-white boundary is lost.

views.label: Neurone and barrier
views.text: Injured neurons and astrocytes swell and endothelial cells leak, adding water to the brain. Cells that lose blood supply swell further.

*.body: The skull is a rigid box. Bleeding or swelling adds volume, pressure rises, and blood flow into the brain falls.
*.care: Helps: Head up 30 degrees; Hypertonic saline; Mannitol. Avoid: Hypotonic fluids; Hypotension or hypoxia.

**.body: Injured neurons and astrocytes swell and endothelial cells leak, adding water to the brain. Cells that lose blood supply swell further.
**.care: Helps: Head up 30 degrees; Hypertonic saline; Mannitol. Avoid: Hypotonic fluids; Hypotension or hypoxia.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible early with osmotherapy, drainage or surgery. Prolonged high pressure causes permanent ischaemic injury.

complications.title: Brain herniation

views.label: Brain
views.text: Tissue is pushed across the midline and down through the tentorial notch. The brainstem is compressed.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Shift of midline structures. Haemorrhage in the midbrain and pons (Duret) marks established herniation.

views.label: Neurone and barrier
views.text: Displaced tissue compresses brainstem neurons and the vessels that supply them. Axons stretch and shear, and ischaemia stops their function.

*.body: The brain is pushed across the midline and down through the tentorium. The pupil dilates, the patient becomes comatose, and breathing and blood pressure change.
*.care: Helps: Hyperosmolar bolus; Brief hyperventilation as a bridge; Emergency craniectomy or evacuation. Avoid: Lumbar puncture; Hypotonic fluids.

**.body: Displaced tissue compresses brainstem neurons and the vessels that supply them. Axons stretch and shear, and ischaemia stops their function.
**.care: Helps: Hyperosmolar bolus; Brief hyperventilation as a bridge; Emergency craniectomy or evacuation. Avoid: Lumbar puncture; Hypotonic fluids.

complications.reversibleText: Time critical. Early reversal can recover the patient; established brainstem compression is usually fatal or severely disabling.

complications.title: Cerebral ischaemia after TBI

views.label: Brain
views.text: Under-perfused brain looks pale in the core and dusky at the edge. The penumbra can still be saved.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: A pale, soft wedge of tissue at the core with a blurred border, then reddened margins.

views.label: Neurone and barrier
views.text: Neurons run out of oxygen and glucose, pumps fail, calcium floods in, and excitotoxic glutamate kills nearby cells.

*.body: Pressure from swelling or low blood pressure reduces blood flow to injured brain. Regions around the injury starve and die.
*.care: Helps: Maintain CPP above 60; Normal oxygen and carbon dioxide; Avoid hypotension. Avoid: Hypotension; Hyperventilation.

**.body: Neurons run out of oxygen and glucose, pumps fail, calcium floods in, and excitotoxic glutamate kills nearby cells.
**.care: Helps: Maintain CPP above 60; Normal oxygen and carbon dioxide; Avoid hypotension. Avoid: Hypotension; Hyperventilation.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible for a short time because of the penumbra, but sustained ischaemia produces infarction.

complications.title: Coagulopathy after TBI

views.label: Soft tissue
views.text: Brain tissue releases tissue factor on injury. That consumes clotting factors and bleeding spreads.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Contusions enlarge and haematoma pools. Bleeding does not seal.

views.label: Capillary wall
views.text: Tissue factor from injured neurons and astrocytes activates the clotting cascade throughout the body. Fibrinolysis rises, platelets are consumed and clots that form are weak.

*.body: Brain tissue is rich in tissue factor. Injury releases it into the blood and uses up platelets and clotting factors, so a contusion can enlarge and bleeding can progress.
*.care: Helps: Tranexamic acid early; Platelets and plasma guided by tests; Fibrinogen replacement. Avoid: Continued anticoagulant or antiplatelet; Large volume crystalloid.

**.body: Tissue factor from injured neurons and astrocytes activates the clotting cascade throughout the body. Fibrinolysis rises, platelets are consumed and clots that form are weak.
**.care: Helps: Tranexamic acid early; Platelets and plasma guided by tests; Fibrinogen replacement. Avoid: Continued anticoagulant or antiplatelet; Large volume crystalloid.

complications.reversibleText: Often reversible if recognised early. Progression of bleeding in a contusion can be fatal.

complications.title: Neurogenic pulmonary oedema

views.label: Lungs
views.text: A surge of catecholamines forces blood into the lungs. Capillaries leak and the lungs are heavy and wet.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pink froth and haemorrhagic fluid. The change can appear within minutes of the brain injury.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: Catecholamines constrict systemic veins and push blood into the lungs. Capillary pressure and permeability rise together, so the wall breaks and fluid floods the alveoli.

*.body: A sudden rise in intracranial pressure triggers a catecholamine surge. The lungs flood within minutes to hours, though the heart and lungs were previously normal.
*.care: Helps: Treat intracranial pressure; Lung protective ventilation with PEEP; Careful diuresis when euvolaemic. Avoid: Large fluid boluses; Delayed control of ICP.

**.body: Catecholamines constrict systemic veins and push blood into the lungs. Capillary pressure and permeability rise together, so the wall breaks and fluid floods the alveoli.
**.care: Helps: Treat intracranial pressure; Lung protective ventilation with PEEP; Careful diuresis when euvolaemic. Avoid: Large fluid boluses; Delayed control of ICP.

complications.reversibleText: Usually resolves within days once the pressure is controlled.

complications.title: Hypoxia during status epilepticus

views.label: Microvessels
views.text: During a seizure breathing is impaired. Blood is dark and tissues are starved of oxygen.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Tissue is dusky and wet. The capillary red cells are unsaturated.

views.label: Capillary
views.text: Seizing neurons and muscles use huge amounts of oxygen. Red cells arrive less saturated, so mitochondria fail and the cells switch to anaerobic metabolism.

*.body: During a seizure the chest muscles contract and breathing is ineffective. The airway is blocked by secretions or the tongue, so oxygen falls while demand is high.
*.care: Helps: Airway positioning and oxygen; Early benzodiazepine; Bag mask ventilation. Avoid: Repeated sedatives without airway support.

**.body: Seizing neurons and muscles use huge amounts of oxygen. Red cells arrive less saturated, so mitochondria fail and the cells switch to anaerobic metabolism.
**.care: Helps: Airway positioning and oxygen; Early benzodiazepine; Bag mask ventilation. Avoid: Repeated sedatives without airway support.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible if the airway and oxygen are restored promptly. Prolonged hypoxia adds to neuronal injury.

complications.title: Aspiration in status epilepticus

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Gastric contents burn the airway. The right lower lobe is the usual site.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Red-brown, wet, consolidated lung with food or acid-damaged mucosa in the bronchi.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: Gastric acid burns the alveolar epithelium and capillary cells. Neutrophils flood in and release enzymes, and fluid enters the air spaces.

*.body: Gastric contents or saliva enter the airway during a seizure. Acid and bacteria injure the lung, causing pneumonitis or pneumonia with low oxygen.
*.care: Helps: Side position and suction; Early airway protection; Antibiotics only if pneumonia develops. Avoid: Oral intake while drowsy; Unprotected deep sedation.

**.body: Gastric acid burns the alveolar epithelium and capillary cells. Neutrophils flood in and release enzymes, and fluid enters the air spaces.
**.care: Helps: Side position and suction; Early airway protection; Antibiotics only if pneumonia develops. Avoid: Oral intake while drowsy; Unprotected deep sedation.

complications.reversibleText: Chemical pneumonitis can recover in days; infection and ARDS can follow.

complications.title: Rhabdomyolysis

views.label: Muscle
views.text: Swollen, tense muscle. Dark, mottled areas have lost their fibres and leak myoglobin.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: The muscle is pale, wet and bulging against the fascia. Dead fibres look dull and tan.

views.label: Muscle fibre
views.text: Energy failure stops the pumps in the muscle membrane. Calcium floods in, enzymes digest the fibre, and the membrane ruptures and spills its contents.

*.body: Continuous muscle contraction and heat break down muscle. Myoglobin, potassium and creatine kinase flood the blood and the urine turns dark.
*.care: Helps: Early IV fluids; Stop the seizure and muscle activity; Cool hyperthermia. Avoid: Suxamethonium; Prolonged high dose propofol.

**.body: Energy failure stops the pumps in the muscle membrane. Calcium floods in, enzymes digest the fibre, and the membrane ruptures and spills its contents.
**.care: Helps: Early IV fluids; Stop the seizure and muscle activity; Cool hyperthermia. Avoid: Suxamethonium; Prolonged high dose propofol.

complications.reversibleText: Muscle regenerates. The danger is acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia, which are preventable with early fluids.

complications.title: Neuronal injury after status epilepticus

views.label: Brain
views.text: Excitotoxic injury hits the hippocampus and cortex first. The surface may look normal at first.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pale, swollen hippocampus and cortical layers. Dead neurones are red and shrunken on microscopy.

views.label: Neurone and barrier
views.text: Repeated firing floods neurons with glutamate and calcium. Mitochondria fail, enzymes digest the cell, and neurons die by excitotoxicity.

*.body: Continuous seizures exhaust the brain. Swelling can appear in the hippocampus and cortex, and survivors may have lasting memory and cognitive loss.
*.care: Helps: Stop the seizure with antiseizure drugs; Maintain oxygen and perfusion; Control temperature. Avoid: Uncontrolled prolonged seizures; Hypotension.

**.body: Repeated firing floods neurons with glutamate and calcium. Mitochondria fail, enzymes digest the cell, and neurons die by excitotoxicity.
**.care: Helps: Stop the seizure with antiseizure drugs; Maintain oxygen and perfusion; Control temperature. Avoid: Uncontrolled prolonged seizures; Hypotension.

complications.reversibleText: Early seizure control limits injury. Neurons lost after prolonged status are not replaced.

complications.title: Bleeding in DIC

views.label: Soft tissue
views.text: Haematoma, petechiae and oozing from every puncture site. Platelets and factors are used up.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Blood pools between tissue planes and cannot be sealed.

views.label: Capillary wall
views.text: Thrombin generation uses up platelets, fibrinogen and factors. Plasmin breaks down the clots that do form, and the vessel wall has nothing to seal it.

*.body: Platelets and clotting factors are consumed, so the patient oozes from lines, wounds, gums and the gut, and may bleed into the brain.
*.care: Helps: Treat the underlying cause; Platelets if bleeding or below 50; Fresh frozen plasma. Avoid: Tranexamic acid in DIC with thrombosis; Heparin in a bleeding patient.

**.body: Thrombin generation uses up platelets, fibrinogen and factors. Plasmin breaks down the clots that do form, and the vessel wall has nothing to seal it.
**.care: Helps: Treat the underlying cause; Platelets if bleeding or below 50; Fresh frozen plasma. Avoid: Tranexamic acid in DIC with thrombosis; Heparin in a bleeding patient.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible once the trigger is controlled. An ongoing trigger sustains the consumption.

complications.title: Microvascular thrombosis in DIC

views.label: Microvessels
views.text: Fibrin plugs fill small vessels. Tissue downstream turns pale and then dusky.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Thrombi in capillaries and arterioles. Bleeding and clotting happen together.

views.label: Capillary
views.text: Tissue factor and injured endothelium start the clotting cascade. Thrombin makes fibrin, platelets stick, and natural anticoagulants such as antithrombin are used up.

*.body: Tiny clots form throughout the small vessels. Skin, kidneys, lungs and brain are damaged, and purpura or gangrene can appear.
*.care: Helps: Treat the trigger; Prophylactic heparin without active bleeding; Antithrombin or thrombomodulin in selected cases. Avoid: Tranexamic acid; Platelets without bleeding.

**.body: Tissue factor and injured endothelium start the clotting cascade. Thrombin makes fibrin, platelets stick, and natural anticoagulants such as antithrombin are used up.
**.care: Helps: Treat the trigger; Prophylactic heparin without active bleeding; Antithrombin or thrombomodulin in selected cases. Avoid: Tranexamic acid; Platelets without bleeding.

complications.reversibleText: Micro clots break down once the trigger is controlled. Large vessel thrombosis and purpura fulminans leave lasting damage.

complications.title: Organ ischaemia in DIC

views.label: Bowel
views.text: Bowel with patchy purple-black segments. Clotted small vessels and low flow starve the wall.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: A dusky, thick wall with haemorrhagic mucosa. Dead segments are sharply demarcated.

views.label: Villus
views.text: Cells downstream of a blocked capillary lose oxygen. Pumps fail, cells swell, switch to anaerobic metabolism and die.

*.body: Clotted small vessels and low pressure starve the kidneys, lungs, liver, brain and skin. Organs begin to fail one after another.
*.care: Helps: Restore perfusion pressure; Treat the trigger; Oxygenation. Avoid: Excess vasopressor; Hypotension.

**.body: Cells downstream of a blocked capillary lose oxygen. Pumps fail, cells swell, switch to anaerobic metabolism and die.
**.care: Helps: Restore perfusion pressure; Treat the trigger; Oxygenation. Avoid: Excess vasopressor; Hypotension.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible while the tissue is only ischaemic; infarcted tissue does not recover.

complications.title: AKI in DIC

views.label: Kidney
views.text: Fibrin clogs the glomerular capillaries. The kidney is pale with red speckles.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pale cortex with dark infarcts. Cortical necrosis is permanent.

views.label: Tubule
views.text: Fibrin plugs the glomerular loops and small arteries. Tubule cells downstream lose oxygen and die, and red cells fragment as they squeeze past the clots.

*.body: Micro clots block the glomerular capillaries and low pressure cuts renal perfusion. Urine output falls, blood may appear in the urine, and creatinine rises.
*.care: Helps: Restore perfusion; Treat the trigger; Avoid nephrotoxins. Avoid: NSAIDs; Contrast in a low flow state.

**.body: Fibrin plugs the glomerular loops and small arteries. Tubule cells downstream lose oxygen and die, and red cells fragment as they squeeze past the clots.
**.care: Helps: Restore perfusion; Treat the trigger; Avoid nephrotoxins. Avoid: NSAIDs; Contrast in a low flow state.

complications.reversibleText: Often reversible if the trigger is controlled. Cortical necrosis from severe thrombosis is permanent.

complications.title: Purpura fulminans

views.label: Skin
views.text: Spreading purple-black patches with blisters. Small vessels in the skin are blocked by thrombi.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Dermis packed with thrombi and extravasated red cells. The epidermis dies above them.

views.label: Skin layers
views.text: Protein C and antithrombin are exhausted, so thrombin and fibrin run unchecked. Skin capillaries are plugged, the endothelium dies, and the skin cells downstream starve.

*.body: Purple, painful patches spread across the skin and limbs. Small vessels in the skin are clotted, so the tissue dies and may become gangrenous.
*.care: Helps: Treat the trigger, such as meningococcus; Protein C or antithrombin replacement; Heparin when no major bleeding. Avoid: High dose vasopressors; Tight dressings or tourniquets.

**.body: Protein C and antithrombin are exhausted, so thrombin and fibrin run unchecked. Skin capillaries are plugged, the endothelium dies, and the skin cells downstream starve.
**.care: Helps: Treat the trigger, such as meningococcus; Protein C or antithrombin replacement; Heparin when no major bleeding. Avoid: High dose vasopressors; Tight dressings or tourniquets.

complications.reversibleText: Early treatment can save skin. Established necrosis needs debridement or amputation.

complications.title: Sepsis: the septic microcirculation

views.label: Microvessel
views.text: A septic arteriole and capillary bed. The vessel is dilated and plasma leaks into the tissue.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Pale, oedematous tissue with congested capillaries.

views.label: Capillary wall
views.text: An activated endothelium that has lost its coat, leaks plasma and displays tissue factor.

*.body: Sepsis, organ level. A dysregulated response to infection dilates vessels and makes the capillaries leak. Pressure and flow fall, tissues are starved of oxygen and lactate rises. Several organs can fail together.
*.care: Helps: Antibiotics within one hour; Source control; Balanced crystalloid; Noradrenaline; Hydrocortisone in refractory shock. Avoid: Delayed antibiotics; Large fluid overload; Starch colloid.

**.body: Sepsis, cell level. Toxins and cytokines switch on the endothelium. It loses its protective coat, leaks plasma, displays tissue factor and promotes micro clots, so oxygen cannot reach the cells.
**.care: Helps: Antibiotics within one hour; Source control; Balanced crystalloid; Noradrenaline; Hydrocortisone in refractory shock. Avoid: Delayed antibiotics; Large fluid overload; Starch colloid.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible if the source is controlled and perfusion is restored early. Late organ damage, such as kidney or brain injury, may only partly recover.

complications.title: ARDS: diffuse alveolar damage

views.label: Lungs
views.text: Heavy, dark red, airless lungs. The back of each lung is solid with fluid and collapse.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Wet, red and rubbery lung that weighs two to three times normal. Frothy fluid weeps from the cut face.

views.label: Alveolus
views.text: A flooded air sac with a hyaline membrane and neutrophils.

*.body: ARDS, organ level. Both lungs fill with protein rich fluid and collapse in the dependent areas. The lung becomes stiff and heavy, leaving a small working baby lung that is easily overstretched.
*.care: Helps: Low tidal volume, 6 ml per kg; Titrated PEEP; Prone positioning; Neuromuscular blockade in severe ARDS; Conservative fluids; VV ECMO for refractory hypoxaemia. Avoid: High tidal volume; Liberal fluids.

**.body: ARDS, cell level. Inflammatory cells damage the alveolar lining and the capillary beneath it. Fluid floods the air sacs, surfactant fails and a hyaline membrane blocks gas exchange.
**.care: Helps: Low tidal volume, 6 ml per kg; Titrated PEEP; Prone positioning; Neuromuscular blockade in severe ARDS; Conservative fluids; VV ECMO for refractory hypoxaemia. Avoid: High tidal volume; Liberal fluids.

complications.reversibleText: Many patients recover most lung function over months. Severe cases leave scarring and weakness.

complications.title: Acute necrotising pancreatitis

views.label: Pancreas
views.text: A swollen gland with chalky white fat necrosis and dark haemorrhagic areas.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Soft, mottled tissue with dead areas, fluid and fat necrosis.

views.label: Acinar cell
views.text: An acinus digesting itself as enzyme granules fuse and spill.

*.body: Acute pancreatitis, organ level. The gland digests itself. It swells, fat around it is destroyed, and the inflammation can reach the lungs, kidneys and circulation.
*.care: Helps: Treat the cause; Moderate Ringer lactate; Early enteral feeding; Analgesia. Avoid: Aggressive fluid loading; Prophylactic antibiotics; Prolonged nil by mouth.

**.body: Acute pancreatitis, cell level. Inside the acinar cell, enzymes are activated too early. They digest the cell and escape through the broken membrane.
**.care: Helps: Treat the cause; Moderate Ringer lactate; Early enteral feeding; Analgesia. Avoid: Aggressive fluid loading; Prophylactic antibiotics; Prolonged nil by mouth.

complications.reversibleText: Mild disease usually recovers fully. Necrosis does not regenerate and may become infected.

complications.title: Acute tubular injury

views.label: Kidney
views.text: A swollen, pale kidney. The cortex bulges and the capsule is tense.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: A pale, swollen cortex against a dark, congested medulla.

views.label: Tubule
views.text: Injured tubular cells lose their brush border and slough into the lumen as casts.

*.body: AKI, organ level. Filtration falls and urine output drops. Urea, potassium and acid build up and fluid is retained.
*.care: Helps: Treat the cause and restore perfusion; Balanced crystalloid if volume depleted; Stop nephrotoxins; Keep MAP at 65 or above; Renal replacement therapy. Avoid: NSAIDs; Aminoglycoside or contrast; Fluid overload.

**.body: AKI, cell level. Tubular cells lose energy, shed their brush border and slough into the lumen. Casts block the tubule and filtration falls.
**.care: Helps: Treat the cause and restore perfusion; Balanced crystalloid if volume depleted; Stop nephrotoxins; Keep MAP at 65 or above; Renal replacement therapy. Avoid: NSAIDs; Aminoglycoside or contrast; Fluid overload.

complications.reversibleText: Often recovers over days to weeks if the cause is removed. Severe or repeated injury can leave chronic kidney disease.

complications.title: Acute liver failure: massive necrosis

views.label: Liver
views.text: A shrunken, soft liver with a wrinkled capsule and yellow-green, mottled areas.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Mottled red, yellow and green cut face with large areas of necrosis.

views.label: Hepatocyte
views.text: Dying hepatocytes with failing mitochondria and no glycogen.

*.body: Acute liver failure, organ level. The liver cannot make clotting factors or clear ammonia. The INR rises, blood sugar falls and the brain swells.
*.care: Helps: N-acetylcysteine; Remove the cause; Lactulose and ammonia control; Renal replacement for ammonia; Emergency transplant listing. Avoid: Late N-acetylcysteine; Sedatives and hepatotoxic drugs.

**.body: Acute liver failure, cell level. Hepatocytes lose energy and their membranes break. Dying cells cannot detoxify ammonia or store glycogen.
**.care: Helps: N-acetylcysteine; Remove the cause; Lactulose and ammonia control; Renal replacement for ammonia; Emergency transplant listing. Avoid: Late N-acetylcysteine; Sedatives and hepatotoxic drugs.

complications.reversibleText: Some patients regenerate fully if the cause is removed early. Others need transplant to survive.

complications.title: Acute decompensated heart failure

views.label: Heart
views.text: A dilated, globular heart with a rounded apex and dilated chambers.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Dilated ventricular cavities with a thin, pale wall and flattened trabeculae.

views.label: Myocyte
views.text: A myocyte with swollen, energy-starved mitochondria.

*.body: Acute heart failure, organ level. The ventricle fails to pump and the heart dilates. Pressure backs up into the lungs and body, and output to the organs falls.
*.care: Helps: IV loop diuretic; Nitrate when blood pressure allows; Non-invasive ventilation; Treat the precipitant; Dobutamine in low output; Mechanical circulatory support. Avoid: Fluid bolus; Beta blocker in low output; NSAIDs.

**.body: Acute heart failure, cell level. Myocytes lose energy and their calcium handling fails, so each cell squeezes with less force.
**.care: Helps: IV loop diuretic; Nitrate when blood pressure allows; Non-invasive ventilation; Treat the precipitant; Dobutamine in low output; Mechanical circulatory support. Avoid: Fluid bolus; Beta blocker in low output; NSAIDs.

complications.reversibleText: Often improves with decongestion and treatment of the trigger. The underlying cardiomyopathy may remain.

complications.title: Traumatic brain injury

views.label: Brain
views.text: A swollen brain with contusions on the frontal and temporal poles and flattened gyri.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Effaced sulci, compressed ventricles and a shift of the midline.

views.label: Neurone
views.text: A swollen neurone and astrocyte after shearing and excitotoxic injury.

*.body: Traumatic brain injury, organ level. The impact bruises and swells the brain inside a fixed skull. Pressure rises, the brain shifts across the midline and perfusion falls.
*.care: Helps: Head up 30 degrees; Hypertonic saline; Sedation and analgesia; CSF drainage; Evacuate a mass lesion; Keep CPP at 60 or above. Avoid: Hypotension; Hypotonic fluids; Hypoxia or hypercapnia.

**.body: Traumatic brain injury, cell level. Shear stretches axons and neurons. Ion pumps fail, cells swell and release excitotoxic transmitters that injure their neighbours.
**.care: Helps: Head up 30 degrees; Hypertonic saline; Sedation and analgesia; CSF drainage; Evacuate a mass lesion; Keep CPP at 60 or above. Avoid: Hypotension; Hypotonic fluids; Hypoxia or hypercapnia.

complications.reversibleText: Primary injury is permanent. Secondary injury from swelling and ischaemia can be prevented or limited.

complications.title: Status epilepticus

views.label: Brain
views.text: A swollen brain with congested cortex, worst in the medial temporal lobes.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Swollen, congested grey matter, with the hippocampus most at risk.

views.label: Neurone
views.text: A neurone fired to exhaustion: swollen, with failing mitochondria and a rising potassium cloud.

*.body: Status epilepticus, organ level. Seizure activity continues for more than five minutes. The brain burns far more oxygen and glucose than it receives, and the body develops fever, acidosis and muscle breakdown.
*.care: Helps: First line benzodiazepine; Second line antiseizure drug; Anaesthetic infusion in refractory status; Treat the cause; Correct glucose and electrolytes. Avoid: Delayed first treatment; Under-dosed benzodiazepine.

**.body: Status epilepticus, cell level. Neurones fire continuously. Glutamate and potassium accumulate, calcium floods in and the cell exhausts its energy and dies.
**.care: Helps: First line benzodiazepine; Second line antiseizure drug; Anaesthetic infusion in refractory status; Treat the cause; Correct glucose and electrolytes. Avoid: Delayed first treatment; Under-dosed benzodiazepine.

complications.reversibleText: Seizures stopped early leave little damage. Long seizures kill neurones and are harder to stop.

complications.title: Disseminated intravascular coagulation

views.label: Microvessel
views.text: Capillaries plugged with fibrin, with oozing at the margins.

views.label: Cut surface
views.text: Mottled tissue with pale infarcts and small haemorrhages.

views.label: Capillary
views.text: Fibrin strands, trapped red cells and platelets inside a damaged capillary.

*.body: DIC, organ level. Clotting is switched on throughout the circulation. Clots block small vessels and starve organs, while the clotting factors and platelets are used up, so the patient also bleeds.
*.care: Helps: Treat the underlying cause; Platelets if bleeding or very low; Plasma or cryoprecipitate if bleeding; Heparin in thrombosis predominant DIC; Natural anticoagulant replacement. Avoid: Tranexamic acid; Invasive procedures without correction.

**.body: DIC, cell level. Tissue factor on the endothelium and inflammatory cells triggers thrombin. Fibrin plugs the capillary, red cells are sheared and platelets are consumed.
**.care: Helps: Treat the underlying cause; Platelets if bleeding or very low; Plasma or cryoprecipitate if bleeding; Heparin in thrombosis predominant DIC; Natural anticoagulant replacement. Avoid: Tranexamic acid; Invasive procedures without correction.

complications.reversibleText: Reversible if the trigger is controlled. Organ damage from micro thrombi and bleeding may be permanent.
